issues.legal_issue: Later amendments to the general land-acquisition law concerning compensation apply to acquisitions made for a statutory housing scheme where the scheme incorporates the earlier law with modifications.
material_facts: Land was acquired for a housing scheme under the state housing statute, which authorized acquisition under the Land Acquisition Act as modified by a schedule to that statute.
The schedule contained modifications concerning acquisition procedure and compensation, including the compensation provisions as they stood when the housing statute was enacted.
A later amendment to the Land Acquisition Act enhanced compensation benefits, and the housing statute was not correspondingly amended.

The court concluded that excluding the later compensation amendments would result in different compensation for owners whose land was acquired by the same acquiring authority under different acquisition routes.
issues.conclusion: The later amendments concerning determination and payment of compensation apply to acquisitions for the purposes of the housing statute.
issues.legal_principle: A statutory reference may incorporate an earlier enactment, in which case subsequent amendments ordinarily do not apply, subject to the exceptions stated in State of Madhya Pradesh v. M.V. Narasimhan, including where the enactments are supplemental or in pari materia, where non-application would make the later enactment unworkable, or where the later amendment expressly or by necessary intendment applies. Applying Secretary of State v. Hindustan Co-operative Insurance Society Ltd., the court treated the acquisition provisions as incorporated. However, Nagpur Improvement Trust v. Vithal Rao establishes that owners cannot be given different compensation merely because land is acquired under different enactments or for different public purposes. The court therefore adopted a construction consistent with Article 14, applying the compensation amendments in Sections 23(1-A), 23(2), and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, as amended in 1984. The court also applied the principle in Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar that, where one construction is constitutional and another is not, the constitutional construction should be preferred.

rule.if: statutory_scheme_acquisition and modified_reference_to_general_acquisition_law and later_compensation_amendments and (same_authority_acquisition or otherwise_unworkable_compensation_scheme)

predicates.statutory_scheme_acquisition: A public authority acquired land to carry out a scheme authorized by a separate statutory enactment.
predicates.modified_reference_to_general_acquisitio: The enactment authorized acquisition under a general acquisition law subject to specified modifications.
predicates.later_compensation_amendments: The general acquisition law was later amended to change the compensation benefits available to landowners.
predicates.same_authority_acquisition: The same acquiring authority could acquire comparable land either under the scheme enactment or under the general acquisition law.
predicates.otherwise_unworkable_compensation_scheme: Without applying the later compensation amendments, the compensation framework for the scheme would produce an unjustifiably different result for similarly situated landowners.

issues.definition: When land is acquired for a statutory scheme under a modified reference to a general acquisition law, later compensation amendments apply if the same authority acquires comparable land by another route or their exclusion would make the compensation framework unjustifiably different.

issues.legal_issue: Applying the earlier, lower compensation benefits to scheme acquisitions would create constitutionally impermissible unequal treatment, so the acquisition provisions should be construed to apply the later compensation amendments.
material_facts: The landowners challenged the scheme-specific acquisition provisions on the ground that they received lower solatium and interest than owners whose land was acquired under the amended general acquisition law.
The court found that acquisition under either route was carried out by the same state authority.
The court construed the scheme statute to apply the later compensation amendments, and consequently held that the constitutional challenge did not survive.
issues.conclusion: The court did not invalidate the scheme provisions; it construed them to apply the later compensation amendments, after which the constitutional challenge did not survive.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not permit different compensation merely because land is acquired under one enactment rather than another where the same authority acquires the land. Nagpur Improvement Trust v. Vithal Rao applied that principle to acquisition statutes providing different compensation. The court distinguished State of Madhya Pradesh v. G.C. Mandawar because the alleged discrimination here arose from action by the same authority, and distinguished Prakash Amichand Shah v. State of Gujarat and Union of India v. Hari Krishan Khosla because they concerned different acquisition arrangements. Under Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar, the court preferred a construction that avoided unconstitutionality. It therefore held that the later amendments to Sections 23(1-A), 23(2), and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act applied, and did not need to decide the separate contention concerning repugnancy under Article 254.

rule.if: statutory_scheme_acquisition and lower_scheme_compensation and same_authority_acquisition and constitutional_construction_available

predicates.statutory_scheme_acquisition: A public authority acquired land to carry out a scheme under a separate statutory enactment.
predicates.lower_scheme_compensation: The scheme's compensation rules, if read without later amendments, would provide lower benefits than those available for comparable acquisitions under the general law.
predicates.same_authority_acquisition: The same acquiring authority could acquire comparable land under either the scheme enactment or the general acquisition law.
predicates.constitutional_construction_available: The scheme enactment can reasonably be construed to extend the later compensation benefits to scheme acquisitions.

issues.definition: Where scheme acquisitions would otherwise receive lower compensation than comparable acquisitions by the same authority, and a constitutionally consistent construction is available, the challenge does not survive because the scheme receives the amended compensation.

issues.legal_issue: The valuation of a large undeveloped tract by reference to small developed-area sales may account for development costs through a deduction, and the appellate valuation and deduction should stand when supported by the evidence.
material_facts: The acquired land covered a large area, was used for agriculture, and was undeveloped, although it lay within municipal limits near developed areas and had development potential and road access.
The landowners relied on sales of small plots in the surrounding developed area, including an exemplar for a small parcel at the rate adopted by the High Court before deduction.
The High Court treated the small-plot sales as guidance rather than as directly equivalent sales, and deducted one third for development costs associated with creating roads and other amenities.
The Supreme Court found no ground to disturb the High Court's market-value assessment or its development deduction.
issues.conclusion: The High Court's valuation, including the deduction for development costs, was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Market value of a large tract may be assessed using sales of smaller parcels as guidance, with a deduction to reflect the difference in size and development costs. The court relied on Kaushalya Devi Bogra v. Land Acquisition Officer, which recognizes deductions when small-property sales are used to value a large property and notes that deductions may vary, including one third. It also relied on Tribeni Devi v. Collector of Ranchi, Vijay Kumar Moti Lal v. State of Maharashtra, Special Land Acquisition Officer, Bangalore v. V.T. Velu, K.S. Shivadevamma v. Assistant Commissioner, and Basant Kumar v. Union of India in upholding a one-third development deduction in the circumstances.

rule.if: appeal_from_compensation_assessment and large_undeveloped_tract and small_parcel_comparables and development_costs_required and supported_appellate_assessment

predicates.appeal_from_compensation_assessment: A party appealed a court's assessment of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.large_undeveloped_tract: The acquired property was a large tract that lacked the development of nearby areas.
predicates.small_parcel_comparables: The valuation evidence included sales of small parcels in developed areas that could provide guidance but were not directly equivalent to the acquired tract.
predicates.development_costs_required: The acquired tract would require development work, such as roads and other amenities, before use as building sites.
predicates.supported_appellate_assessment: The appellate court's valuation and allowance for development costs were supported by the evidence and relevant circumstances.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a compensation assessment, a supported valuation of a large undeveloped tract may rely on small-parcel sales as guidance and allow a deduction for necessary development costs.

issues.legal_issue: Agreements to sell that are not shown to have resulted in completed sales may be rejected as additional evidence when they do not assist in determining the market value of acquired land.
material_facts: The acquiring authority sought permission in the High Court to introduce agreements to sell as additional evidence in the compensation appeals.
There was no material showing that the agreements had matured into sale transactions, and the High Court found them unhelpful in determining market value.
The Supreme Court found no substance in the challenge to the rejection of that evidence.
issues.conclusion: The rejection of the agreements to sell as additional evidence was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Evidence of agreements to sell may be of little assistance in determining market value where there is no material showing that the agreements resulted in completed sale transactions. The court applied that evidentiary assessment to uphold the High Court's rejection of the proposed additional evidence.

rule.if: appeal_from_compensation_assessment and proposed_additional_evidence_is_sale_agreements and no_completed_sale_shown and evidence_does_not_assist_market_value

predicates.appeal_from_compensation_assessment: A party appealed a court's assessment of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.proposed_additional_evidence_is_sale_agr: A party sought to introduce agreements to sell as additional evidence in the compensation proceedings.
predicates.no_completed_sale_shown: The party did not provide material showing that the agreements resulted in completed sales.
predicates.evidence_does_not_assist_market_value: The proposed evidence was found not to assist in determining the market value of the acquired land.

issues.definition: In a compensation appeal, agreements to sell may be rejected as additional evidence when no completed sales are shown and the agreements do not assist in determining market value.
